Claude
12:47 UTC, 6 April 2026
Searched the web for “Wyoming LLC annual report filing fee 2025”
Here's a rundown of each question:
Annual report — yes, required. Wyoming LLCs must file an annual report with the Wyoming Secretary of State, due on the first day of the anniversary month of your LLC's formation. So if ZenBusiness formed it in, say, March, your report is due March 1 every year. Check your formation date in the Wyoming Business Database if you're not sure.
The fee. It's $60 (plus a $2 convenience fee for online payment), or $0.0002 × your Wyoming asset value, whichever is greater. For most single-member LLCs with minimal in-state assets, you're looking at $62 total. You file directly through the Wyoming Secretary of State website — it's a simple online wizard.
ZenBusiness. They handle your registered agent service and compliance reminders, but they don't do your taxes. They're a formation/compliance service, not a tax preparer. They may send you a reminder when the annual report is due (and offer to file it for a fee), but that's separate from anything IRS-related.
FreeTaxUSA. This depends entirely on how your LLC is taxed federally. If it's a single-member LLC, it's a disregarded entity by default — you report business income/expenses on Schedule C of your personal 1040, and FreeTaxUSA handles that fine. If it's a multi-member LLC (taxed as a partnership), you'd need to file Form 1065 first, and FreeTaxUSA doesn't support 1065s — you'd need something like TaxAct or a CPA for that piece. The Wyoming annual report is a state compliance filing, not a tax return, so FreeTaxUSA isn't involved there at all.

Correct, the annual report is purely a state compliance filing — keeps the LLC in good standing, has nothing to do with the IRS.
For a partnership LLC, your tax situation is:
Form 1065 (federal partnership return) — this is the LLC's own filing, due March 15. It doesn't result in tax owed directly; it produces Schedule K-1s for each partner showing their share of income/loss.
Each partner's personal 1040 — you each report your K-1 income there, and that's where the actual tax gets paid.
FreeTaxUSA doesn't support 1065, so you'll need something else for that piece. The main options are TaxAct (cheapest, ~$110 for a partnership return), TurboTax Business (Windows desktop only, ~$170), or a CPA. If the partnership is between you and Ana and the financials are relatively straightforward, TaxAct is probably the right call. A CPA makes more sense if there are complications — cross-border income, multiple income streams being routed through it, etc.
One thing worth flagging: March 15 has already passed for tax year 2025. If you haven't filed yet, you'll want to file Form 7004 to get an automatic 6-month extension (moves the deadline to September 15). That's quick to do and avoids late-filing penalties on the 1065. The extension is for filing only — any tax owed was technically due March 15, but at the partnership level there's usually no tax owed directly.

Claude
12:53 UTC, 6 April 2026
Yes, it matters, though the core filing obligation (Form 1065) is the same. The main wrinkle is withholding.
If Ana is a non-resident alien (NRA) and received a share of partnership income that's "effectively connected income" (ECI) — meaning income from a US trade or business — the partnership is required to withhold and remit tax on her behalf using Form 8804/8805. The withholding rate is 37% for individuals. This is the partnership's obligation, not hers personally.
If she's a resident alien for tax purposes (i.e., she passes the substantial presence test or has a green card), she's treated essentially the same as a US citizen and the withholding rules don't apply.
The other thing worth knowing: non-resident alien partners technically require a US ITIN or SSN to be listed on the K-1. If she doesn't have one, that's a complication.
Practically speaking, given the complexity — foreign partner, late filing, potential withholding obligations — this is probably a situation where paying a CPA to sort out the 1065 is worth it. The cost of getting the 8804/8805 wrong or missing it entirely is higher than a CPA's fee.
A few questions that would sharpen the picture:
Is Ana a US resident for tax purposes, or non-resident?
Does she have an ITIN or SSN?
What kind of income is flowing through the LLC — is it US-sourced?

So the "she was just a contractor" framing doesn't hold up on a 1065. You can't deduct payments to a partner the way you'd deduct a contractor expense.

Ana's ITIN is technically required. The K-1 requires ITINs for a 1065 partnership return to be filed correctly. If no SSN exists, the partner must file Form W-7 to obtain an ITIN so the partnership can declare their share of income/losses on the partnership return.

If the ITIN is not received before the due date of the Form 1065, the partnership can enter "applied for" and the application date on the K-1 issued to the partner. The good news on withholding. A partnership must pay withholding tax on a foreign partner's distributive share only when it has effectively connected taxable income allocable to that foreign partner. Since Ana's services are performed entirely in Georgia and the income is foreign-sourced, there's no ECI, so the 8804/8805 withholding obligation almost certainly doesn't apply to you.
The practical path forward:
Start Ana's ITIN application (Form W-7) immediately — it takes 6-11 weeks, sometimes longer
File Form 7004 to extend the 1065 to September 15
File Form 4868 to extend your personal return to October 15
File the 1065 with "applied for" if the ITIN doesn't arrive in time
The ITIN is a real requirement but not an immediate blocker given the extension. Start the W-7 process now in parallel.

Claude
14:54 UTC, 6 April 2026
The K-1 is an output of preparing the 1065, not a separate thing you file independently. Here's how it works mechanically:
When you (or a CPA, or tax software) prepare the Form 1065, the software automatically generates a Schedule K-1 for each partner as part of that process. You don't fill out K-1s separately — they're produced by the 1065 preparation.
So the workflow is:
You enter all the LLC's income and expenses into the 1065
The software allocates everything between partners according to ownership percentages
It spits out a K-1 for you and a K-1 for Ana
You take your K-1 and use it to fill out your personal 1040
The K-1 is essentially just a summary document — your slice of the partnership's financials — that the 1065 preparation produces automatically.
This is why the 1065 is the bottleneck. You can't have a K-1 without first doing the 1065. And it's also why software like TaxAct Business (which supports 1065) is the DIY route, versus FreeTaxUSA which only does personal returns. TaxAct Business would walk you through the 1065 and generate both K-1s as part of that process.
So to directly answer your question — you generate it yourself through the 1065 preparation process, or a CPA does it for you. Either way it comes out the other end of that process.

So your structure sits exactly where Congress drew that line. The fact that it's tax-efficient for Ana isn't suspicious — it's the system working as designed.

Mail — you literally print the form, fill it out, put it in an envelope and mail it to an IRS address. Old school but completely valid.
E-file — you submit it electronically through a website. Either directly through IRS.gov (called "Free File") or through tax software like FreeTaxUSA, TurboTax, TaxAct etc. The software asks you questions, fills in the form behind the scenes, and transmits it to the IRS.
Through a preparer — a CPA or tax preparer does all of this for you.

The §121 certification Doug signed at closing was technically inaccurate
He would need to file Schedule D and Form 8949 reporting the full sale, claiming the $250k exclusion, and paying capital gains tax on the excess
He does not need to amend anything with the title company — that's their filing obligation, not his
The IRS may never know unless he reports it, but if the gain exceeds $250k he is legally required to report it regardless of whether a 1099-S exists

No — the amount deposited in your account is not the gain. That's the net proceeds after paying off your mortgage, agent commissions, closing costs, and any other fees. The gain is calculated differently:
Gain = Sale price − Original purchase price − Selling costs − Improvement costs
The sale price is the gross number before any of those deductions. What landed in your bank account already has the mortgage payoff and fees removed, so it's not a useful starting point for the gain calculation.
On finding the closing disclosure:
This is the key document — it shows the full sale price, every fee, every deduction, and exactly how the proceeds were distributed. Three places to look:
Email from your real estate attorney or title company — closing disclosures are almost always sent electronically now
DocuSign or similar — if you signed closing documents electronically, there's likely an email with a link to the full document package
Your real estate attorney directly — they keep copies of everything and can send it immediately
The original 2019 purchase documents are similar — either in your email from when you bought the house, or your attorney at the time would have them.

Claude
11:06 UTC, 13 April 2026
No — the money given to you was the net proceeds, not the gain. Here's why:
When you sold, the closing process worked roughly like this:
text
Sale price (what buyer paid)
− Mortgage payoff (what Chase got)
− Agent commission (~5-6%)
− Closing costs and fees
= Net proceeds (what landed in your account)
The gain is a completely separate calculation:
text
Sale price
− What you originally paid in 2019
− Improvements made during ownership
− Selling costs (commission, fees)
= Gain (what the IRS taxes)
So for example if you bought for $400k in 2019, sold for $650k in 2025, paid $40k in commission and fees, your gain is $210k — completely under the $250k exclusion and tax free. But what landed in your account depends on how much mortgage you had left, which has nothing to do with the gain calculation.
The mortgage payoff is irrelevant to the IRS. They don't care what you owed Chase — they care what you made above what you originally paid.
So the key numbers we actually need are:
What did you pay for the house in 2019?
What was the gross sale price in December 2025?
Do you know either of those off the top of your head?

Here's the complete honest picture after thorough research:
The 50% allocation is correct and cannot be changed for 2025. Here's why, and what the limits are:
What would allow more than 50%:
Partnerships can allocate tax items differently than ownership percentages IF the allocation has "substantial economic effect" under Section 704(b). This means the operating agreement must explicitly specify the special allocation, it must have been in place before the tax year, and the allocation must reflect real economic reality — not just a tax benefit shift.
You don't have that in place for 2025, so retroactively claiming more than 50% would not survive IRS scrutiny.
What's already working in your favor:
The structure is actually already optimized in the most important way. The guaranteed payment to Ana — $11,227 — is fully deductible by the LLC before the 50/50 split even occurs. So Ana's compensation is already flowing out of the LLC entirely, reducing the income base that gets split. You're not splitting $14,617 of revenue 50/50 — you're splitting a net loss after her payment comes out first. That's the correct and optimal structure.
Your basis is not a problem: A partner can only claim losses up to the amount of their investment (basis) in the partnership. Your $16,000 in capital contributions gives you more than enough basis to absorb your ~$6,078 share of the loss. No limitation applies.
Going forward: If you want Doug to absorb a larger share of losses in future years, you'd need a formal operating agreement with a §704(b) special allocation clause specifying that Doug absorbs a greater percentage of losses commensurate with the fact that he provides all capital contributions. That would be legitimate and defensible. But it has to be prospective, not retroactive.
The bottom line for 2025: ~$6,078 loss on your K-1. It's real money — at your marginal rate on the IRA income, it saves you roughly $700-900 in federal tax plus NY state savings on top. Not nothing.

Critical finding 1: Rev Proc 84-35 does NOT apply to you.
This is the standard penalty abatement route for small partnerships. The partnership must consist entirely of US resident individuals or the estate of a deceased partner. Ana is a nonresident alien. That one fact disqualifies you from Rev Proc 84-35 entirely. This is a real limitation I want you to know about upfront.
Critical finding 2: Filing Form 7004 now won't grant an extension.
Form 7004 must generally be filed on or before the due date of the applicable tax return. March 15 has passed. A late 7004 does not grant a valid extension. The correct path now is to file the 1065 directly as fast as possible to stop the penalty from accumulating further.
The penalty situation:
The IRS assesses a penalty of $245 per partner, per month, for returns due after 12/31/2024, up to 12 months. With 2 partners that's $490 per month. We're approximately one month past the deadline already — so roughly $490 is accruing now and another $490 will accrue on April 15.
The good news — reasonable cause argument:
The penalty can be waived if the entity can show reasonable cause for not filing on time. Do not attach an explanation when you file your return — if you receive a penalty notice, send the IRS an explanation and they will determine if you meet reasonable-cause criteria.
Your reasonable cause argument is genuinely strong:
This is the first tax year of the LLC's existence (formed April 2025)
You genuinely believed the deadline was April 15, not March 15 — a common and understandable mistake for first-time partnership filers
You have a foreign partner situation that complicates the return
You are actively working to file correctly and completely
If this is the first late filing or an anomaly, the IRS may grant relief once — but only once.
You do NOT attach this explanation to the return. File the 1065 cleanly. If and when you receive a penalty notice (CP162A or CP162B), respond to it with the reasonable cause letter citing these facts.
Critical finding 3: This is a short tax year.
The LLC was formed April 15, 2025, members effective April 22, 2025. The first tax year runs approximatelyApril 22 – December 31, 2025. Q1 — 1065 line numbering: Team is correct. Line 22 = Total deductions, Line 23 = Ordinary loss. My guide was off by one. Lines 24–32 are all $0/blank for our filing — confirm: no look-back interest, no BBA, no taxes owed at the partnership level.
Q2 — Schedule B Q19: My guide was wrong. Q19 = NO. The question asks about payments that would require Form 1042-S — i.e., US-source FDAP payments to a foreign person subject to §1441/§1446 withholding. Ana's guaranteed payment is for services performed entirely outside the US, making it foreign-sourced. Foreign-source income paid to a foreign person is not US-source FDAP and is not subject to withholding. No Form 1042-S, no Form 1042. Q19 = No.
Q3 — Schedule B Q30: NO. The LLC never transacted in crypto. Doug's Coinbase/IB activity is entirely on his personal 1040. The Q30 digital asset question refers to the partnership's activity.
Q4 — Schedule B default: Yes, confirmed. For all questions not explicitly addressed (Q11–13a, 14, 17, 18, 20–29, 32): default No. The LLC is a simple domestic two-person service partnership. None of those questions apply.
Q5 — Schedule D Box H/K placement: The team's suggestion is wrong, and my original algorithm was right. Box H → Schedule D Line 2, not Line 3. Box K → Schedule D Line 9, not Line 10. Here is the correct mapping per the 2025 Form 8949 instructions, confirmed from IRS source:
Box A (1099-B, basis reported) → Schedule D Line 1b
Box B (1099-B, basis NOT reported) → Schedule D Line 2
Box C (no form at all) → Schedule D Line 3
Box G (1099-DA, basis reported) → Schedule D Line 1b
Box H (1099-DA, basis NOT reported) → Schedule D Line 2
Box I (digital asset, no form) → Schedule D Line 3
Box E (1099-B LT, basis NOT reported) → Line 9
Box K (1099-DA LT, basis NOT reported) → Line 9
Box L (digital asset LT, no form) → Line 10
Box H is the digital-asset analog of Box B, not Box C. Box C/I are for transactions with no broker form whatsoever. Coinbase issued a 1099-DA — that's a form — so the transactions are reported, basis just wasn't transmitted to the IRS for 2025. Box H, Line 2. The team conflated "basis not reported" with "no form."
Q6 — IT-204 Section 7 per-line numbers: Updating the guide below with the full line table.
Q7 — IT-204 Sections 4/5 (balance sheets, M-1/M-2): The small partnership exception that exempts Schedules L, M-1, and M-2 on the federal 1065 (Schedule B Q4) carries through to the NY IT-204. NY instructions follow the federal exception for partnerships qualifying under Q4. Sections 4 and 5 should be left blank. If the form requires an entry, enter $0 and attach a note: "Small partnership exception under Schedule B Q4 applies — balance sheet and reconciliation schedules not required."
Q8 — IT-204-IP column A vs B: Confirmed. Column A = federal K-1 amounts, Column B = $0 (NY source). My guide saying "all = 0" was misleading and wrong. Column A must have the federal numbers.
Q9 — IT-201 Line 9: Yes, $46,500. NY IT-201 has a separate Line 9 specifically for IRA distributions. It does not simply absorb into federal AGI flow. Enter $46,500 explicitly.
Q10 — IT-201 Line 28: $0. Arthur confirmed earlier that Doug's $19.93 IB interest is described as "broker credit interest" — this is interest earned on cash in the brokerage account, not interest from US Treasury bonds or US government obligations. Line 28 = $0.
Q11 — IT-201 Line 81 (NY underpayment penalty): Almost certainly applies. Doug had zero NY withholding on the $46,500 IRA distribution and made no estimated tax payments. NY's safe harbor requires paying the lesser of 100% of prior year NY tax or 90% of current year NY tax. With no payments at all, a penalty is likely. The team should compute it using NY Form IT-2105.9 (Underpayment of Estimated Tax by Individuals). The penalty rate for 2025 is approximately 7.5–8% annualized on the underpayment. Arthur should calculate this after the NY tax liability is computed and insert it on Line 81. Do not leave blank.
Q12 — K-3 notice wording: Confirmed as correct. Attach the notice from the guide to both K-1s.
Q13 — W-7 missing fields: These must come from Ana directly — passport number, expiration date, city of birth, gender. Cannot proceed without them. Doug needs to request these from Ana now.

Two separate things, neither is about 2025 taxes.
Hours documentation — what it is and why it matters
The LLC lost $6,863 last year. That loss can reduce your other taxable income — but only if the IRS considers you an active participant in the business, not a passive investor. The dividing line is roughly 100 hours of real involvement in the year.
If you can't show 100 hours, the loss gets suspended — it doesn't disappear, but it can't be used until the LLC has future profits. Given the tax benefit at stake, it's worth documenting.
What the team needs from you: a rough reconstruction of your time spent on LLC business in 2025. Not a timesheet — just a written narrative. For example: setting up Mercury and banking, managing the GoDaddy domain, reviewing payments and finances each month, communicating about business direction, handling all the IRS and tax matters including this entire process. Estimate how many hours each category took. Anything you can point to — emails, calendar entries, bank login history — helps if you're ever audited, but a written summary is sufficient to file.
Capital loss carryover — what it is and why it matters
When you sell investments at a loss in a given year and those losses exceed your gains, you can only deduct $3,000 of the excess against ordinary income. The rest carries forward to the next year and reduces your gains then.
The question is: did your 2024 tax return show any unused capital losses on Schedule D? If yes, those reduce your 2025 capital gains and lower your tax bill.
What the team needs: look at your 2024 Form 1040 return — the one you filed for tax year 2024. Find Schedule D. Look at Line 21 (it says "If loss, enter the loss here and on Form 1040..."). If there's a number there, tell the team what it is. If you don't have your 2024 return handy, the team may be able to pull it from the IRS transcripts they already have access to.

Self-filing is completely normal and the IRS has no problem with it. Millions of people do it. There is no flag, no elevated audit risk, and no requirement to use a CPA or software. The IRS literally provides all the forms for free specifically so people can file themselves.
On the "third party designee" question — that's what you saw. It asks if you want to allow someone else (a preparer, accountant, or other person) to discuss the return with the IRS on your behalf. You check No and leave the rest of that section blank. That's the correct answer for a self-prepared return. It doesn't trigger anything.
On the paid preparer section — at the bottom of Form 1040 and Form 1065 there's a block for a paid preparer's name, PTIN, firm, etc. Leave all of it completely blank. That's correct for self-prepared returns.
One thing worth knowing: because you're filing on paper rather than electronically, the IRS will process it by hand which takes longer — sometimes months for a refund or acknowledgment. That's normal for paper. If you owe, send payment with the return to avoid interest accruing. If the IRS has questions they'll mail you a letter to your address on the return, which goes to the Sanford NC forwarding address.
The partnership return (1065) is a slightly different story — partnerships with more than 100 partners are required to e-file, but you have two partners, so paper is fine.
Nothing about this filing is unusual enough to draw attention. Self-prepared, paper-filed, first-year partnership with a short tax year and a foreign partner — the IRS sees all of this routinely.

This is a substantive legal question with real risk implications. I'm going to address all six questions directly, based on the statutory text, Treasury regulations, and relevant Tax Court cases.
Q1 — Does he qualify? Is the job-hopping history disqualifying?
The statute requires being "unable to engage in any substantial gainful activity by reason of any medically determinable physical or mental impairment which can be expected to result in death or to be of long-continued and indefinite duration."
Two critical regulatory clarifications:
First, "substantial gainful activity" refers to "the activity, or a comparable activity, in which the individual customarily engaged prior to the arising of the disability." This is actually a more favorable standard than SSA's. The IRS will examine whether your impairments prevent you from engaging in your customary work activity or any work activity comparable to it — so you don't necessarily need to be unfit for all work, just work similar to what you customarily did before you became disabled.
Second, the disability does not need to be permanent. But it must be "indefinite" — meaning it cannot reasonably be anticipated that the impairment will, in the foreseeable future, be so diminished as no longer to prevent substantial gainful activity.
On the job-hopping history: this cuts both ways. The argument for Doug is that the serial job-hopping was itself a manifestation of the bipolar condition — that even during "medicated stability," he never achieved sustained professional employment. The psychiatrists' theory that the stable period was characterized by hypomania or episodic function rather than genuine stability supports this framing. Under that theory, Doug never truly attained consistent customary gainful activity, and the recent decompensation represents a worsening to the point of total inability to function even at that limited level.
The argument against Doug — and this is the real risk — is that 10 years of medication stability is evidence the condition is remediable. The impairment cannot be diminished, given reasonable effort and safety to the individual, to the extent that it will allow the individual to engage in his customary or any comparable substantial gainful activity. If he was stable on medication for a decade, the IRS can argue the condition is manageable and therefore not of "indefinite duration" preventing SGA. This is the strongest IRS counterargument and the one Tax Court has used to deny the exception in cases involving treatable conditions.
The SSA pending application actually somewhat undercuts the "remediable" argument — you don't apply for permanent disability benefits if you believe your condition is temporary.
Bottom line on Q1: The claim is legally available and has arguable merit, but it is not a clean win. The "indefinite duration" prong is genuinely contested on these facts. I'd characterize it as a moderate-risk position, not a frivolous one.
Q2 — Physician statement requirements and timing
Disability at the time of disbursement, not at the time of the request for the disbursement, is the crucial point in determining whether the waiver applies.
The team needs to know: what was the distribution date on the 1099-R? If the distribution occurred before the manic episode decompensation, the claim becomes much harder to sustain — you cannot retroactively become disabled. If the distribution occurred during or after the acute episode, it is cleaner.
The physician statement must:
Identify the specific medically determinable impairment (bipolar disorder, diagnosis date)
State that Doug is unable to engage in substantial gainful activity comparable to his prior customary occupation
State that the condition is expected to be of long-continued and indefinite duration
Preferably reference the language of §72(m)(7) directly — the statement should confirm that Doug "is disabled as that term is defined in Internal Revenue Code Section 72(m)(7)" meaning "unable to engage in any substantial gainful activity due to a medically determinable physical or mental impairment, which can be expected to result in death or to be of long-continued and indefinite duration."
Include the onset date of the current disabling episode and confirm it preceded the distribution
The statement does not need to be filed with the return. You just need to have it in your possession when you take the exception on your tax return.
Q3 — SSA pending application: neutral, positive, or risk factor?
Positive, with a caveat. A pending SSA application signals good faith — you're not claiming disability for tax purposes while simultaneously asserting fitness for work to SSA. It corroborates the position.
The caveat: The IRS does not automatically accept a disability determination made by the Social Security Administration as sufficient proof. While an SSA determination is highly persuasive, the IRA owner must still ensure their medical evidence specifically meets the language of the IRC. SSA uses "any work" while IRS uses "customary or comparable work" — the IRS standard is easier on this dimension. A future SSA approval would be strong supporting evidence but is not required and will not arrive before filing.
A pending application with no determination is neutral-to-positive. It is not a risk factor.
Q4 — Documentation to retain (not filed — for audit defense)
Retain in a dedicated file:
Treating psychiatrists' signed statements explicitly tracking the §72(m)(7) language, with onset date of current episode
Hospitalization records (dates and facilities for both prior hospitalizations)
Any documentation showing employment history — the job record actually supports the claim if it shows inability to maintain sustained employment
The SSA application and any correspondence
A personal narrative from Doug describing the current episode, its impact on daily functioning, and why he took the distribution
Any financial records showing why the distribution was necessary at the time
Q5 — Relevant case law on similar fact patterns
There is no Tax Court case precisely on point with bipolar disorder and a long intermittent work history. The closest analogous cases involve physical conditions. The relevant holdings are:
In a Tax Court case involving a boiler mechanic diagnosed with hepatitis C, the taxpayer was denied the exception because, even though the illness prevented work during treatment, he failed to show it was "expected to continue for a long and indefinite period." This is the fact pattern most threatening to Doug's claim — a treatable condition where the taxpayer was working before and after the acute phase.
More favorably, in Rideaux, a boiler mechanic was allowed to claim the disability exception when his disability was indefinite because it was impossible to predict when he would be able to resume working. This is the analogy Doug should lean into — the unpredictability of bipolar cycling, particularly after a severe episode following apparent stability, supports an "impossible to predict" argument.
In Trainito, the Tax Court held that a taxpayer must provide proper evidence that, at the date of an early distribution, he was suffering from a disability that prevented his customary gainful activity. The date of disability relative to the distribution date is what matters.
The Chief Counsel Advice 200922041 established that the individual must show they were unable to work in the year of the distribution at any activity comparable to their customary occupation. This is the standard the physicians' statements need to address directly.
Q6 — Realistic downside if the IRS challenges and wins
The worst case is:
The $4,650 penalty is reinstated
Interest accrues from the original due date (roughly 7-8% annually)
The §6662 accuracy-related penalty of 20% of the underpayment applies only if the IRS can show negligence or disregard of rules
On the accuracy-related penalty specifically: no accuracy-related penalty may be imposed on any portion of an underpayment if there was reasonable cause for, and the taxpayer acted in good faith with respect to, such portion. With a physician statement in hand, a pending SSA claim, and a colorable legal argument, this is a reasonable cause / good faith position. The most important factor is the extent of the taxpayer's effort to assess the taxpayer's proper tax liability. Having documented the medical basis, researched the standard, and obtained professional opinions satisfies that test.
Realistic worst case: $4,650 + ~$350 interest (one year) = ~$5,000. The accuracy-related penalty ($930) is defensible on reasonable cause grounds given the documentation. This is not a fraud risk, not a large-dollar audit risk, and not a position that creates downstream exposure.
Expert summary and recommendation
The claim is available, has medical support, has arguable legal merit, and the downside is bounded. The primary risk is the "indefinite duration" prong given the decade of medication stability. That risk is substantially mitigated if:
The physician statements specifically address why the current episode represents a qualitative change from prior functioning, and why the prognosis is indefinite
The distribution date postdates the onset of the current acute episode
The hospitalization history and SSA application are documented
If those three conditions are met, I would assess this as a defensible position worth taking. The penalty savings ($4,650) equals the risk on the table, and the documentation effort needed to defend it is straightforward.
If the distribution date preceded the acute episode, the claim becomes significantly harder and I would not recommend it.
Action item for the team: Confirm the exact distribution date from the 1099-R and compare it to the timeline of the manic episode. That single fact determines whether this is a strong position or a weak one.

On the statement — yes, you can get it now or when you need it. You don't file it with the return, you just need it in your possession before you file. So the practical sequence is: file the return with code 03, have the physician statement ready, keep it with your records. If the IRS ever questions it, you produce it. Most returns claiming code 03 are never questioned.
On the business contradiction — this is a genuinely good observation and worth thinking through carefully, but I don't think it creates a real conflict. Here's why:
The IRS standard asks whether you can engage in your customary or comparable activity. Your customary activity was professional employment — graduate school, business world, sustained career. That is what ended in hospitalizations. The LLC is something categorically different: a small creative business you built around your constraints, not a return to the kind of sustained professional engagement your condition prevents. It generated $14,000 in revenue over 8 months, ran at a loss, and depended heavily on Ana's labor.
More importantly, the material participation claim and the disability claim are answering different questions. Material participation asks whether you were sufficiently involved in the business to make the loss deductible. Disability asks whether you can sustain gainful employment. You can be involved in something without it constituting substantial gainful activity — especially when that involvement produces a net loss and depends on a partner to function.
The statement from your psychiatrists should reflect this nuance: that you have been attempting to build an adapted working arrangement precisely because conventional employment has been closed to you by the condition, and that this attempt has not constituted sustainable gainful activity.
That is not a contradiction. That is actually the story of someone navigating a disability.

Legal basis: Bipolar disorder is a medically determinable mental impairment of long-continued and indefinite duration. Doug's entire adult work history — two psychiatric hospitalizations triggered by professional engagement, serial inability to sustain employment — constitutes the factual record. Correct — for two reasons.
First, the §72(t) penalty is a federal-only construct. New York has no equivalent early withdrawal penalty of its own. NY never charged you the $4,650 in the first place, so eliminating it at the federal level has nothing to subtract at the state level.
Second, NY income tax is computed on the IRA distribution as ordinary income regardless. The $46,500 flows into NY taxable income the same way whether or not the federal penalty applies. The disability exception touches only the penalty line, not the income.
So NY's number doesn't move. You owe NY tax on $46,500 of IRA income either way — the only question was always the federal penalty.

Two things confirmed.
On NY IT-204 — yes it's free. A partnership with no income, gain, loss, or deduction from New York sources who is filing solely because it has a New York resident partner does not owe a filing fee. That's exactly this LLC's situation. No NY source income, filing only because Doug is a NY resident partner. The IT-204 itself costs nothing to file.
On whether a business that made no money has to pay to file — yes, and here's why.
The $179.99 is not a tax. It's the fee charged by the software platform to transmit the return to the IRS. The IRS doesn't provide a free filing path for Form 1065 the way it does for personal 1040s. Every authorized e-file provider charges for the transmission service.
The 1065 is an information return — it doesn't matter that the LLC had no profit. The IRS requires it because it needs the K-1s to verify that Doug and Ana each reported their share correctly on their personal returns. The obligation to file exists the moment there are two or more partners, regardless of income. The penalty for not filing also applies regardless of income — it's purely about the failure to provide information.
It is genuinely frustrating and the cost feels disproportionate for a loss-making LLC in its first year. But the situation is: $179.99 to file now, versus $510/month in penalty until it's filed, and a reasonable cause letter when the penalty notice arrives.
Recommendation stands: TaxZerone at $179.99, then IT-204 free afterward.

This means if Ana were already physically inside the US, the green card process through adjustment of status could proceed. The ban affects consular processing abroad, not adjustment of status from within the US.

Tourist entry: B-2 blocked for new applications.
Spouse green card: Immigrant visa processing suspended indefinitely. The only current path would be if Ana entered the US on a still-valid pre-2026 visa and filed for adjustment of status from inside the country.

This is genuinely promising for Ana. Let me give you the full picture clearly.
The O-1B path for Ana as an illustrator
Illustrator is explicitly listed as a qualifying profession for O-1B. The standard is "distinction" — not world-famous, just substantially above average in the field. You must either have a major international award, or meet at least three of six criteria. Most creative professionals, especially designers, qualify by satisfying three or more of these criteria.
The six criteria include things like: critical reviews or press coverage in major publications, leading role in distinguished projects, high compensation relative to peers, recognition from experts in the field, and commercial success. Ana's Fiverr business, client work, and any press or recognition she's received all count as evidence.
The green card pathway from O-1B
While the O-1B is a nonimmigrant visa, it is considered "dual intent" in practice, meaning holding an O-1B does not prevent you from seeking permanent residency. Two of the most common immigrant pathways for O-1B holders are the EB-1A and the EB-2 NIW, both of which allow for self-petitioning, eliminating the need for a permanent job offer.
The EB-1A is essentially the same evidentiary criteria as the O-1B but a higher standard — if she qualifies for one, building toward the other is natural. The EB-2 NIW focuses more on the national importance of her work.
The kids
O-3 visas exist specifically for the spouse or children of O-1 visa holders. The kids would come on O-3s tied to Ana's O-1B. They travel together, they're covered together.
The one obstacle that remains
Ana still needs a US-based petitioner to file on her behalf — she cannot self-petition for the O-1B itself. A US agent is common for freelance artists — an individual or company that represents her while she works for multiple clients. Your LLC could potentially serve this role, which is worth discussing with an immigration attorney.
Summary of the path:
Build Ana's O-1B case — document her achievements, get an advisory opinion from an arts peer group, find a US petitioner (potentially the LLC)
Ana and kids enter on O-1B + O-3 visas
Once inside, pursue adjustment of status (I-485) for the green card — not subject to the consular freeze
You file an I-130 spousal petition simultaneously to establish the family relationship basis
This is a real path. It requires an immigration attorney to execute properly, but the pieces are there. The most important first step is having an attorney assess Ana's portfolio and client history against the O-1B criteria.

Yes — and this is genuinely good news. Here's what the research confirms:
An agent can act as petitioner on behalf of an applicant. The O-1B visa identifies an agent as either the actual employer of the beneficiary, the representative of both the employer and the beneficiary, or a person or entity authorized by the employer to act as its agent. The agent can be an individual, a company, or an organization that has an agreement with the beneficiary to represent the O-1B applicant as the petitioner.
So you — as an individual US person — can be Ana's agent petitioner. The LLC can too. Either works.
One important rule: immigration rules strictly forbid the beneficiary from acting as both the petitioner and beneficiary. No self-petitioning allowed. Ana can't file for herself. But you filing for her is completely legitimate.
What the petition needs to include:
Form I-129
A contract between you and Ana outlining the work arrangement and compensation
A detailed itinerary of her planned projects and engagements in the US
An advisory opinion letter from a relevant peer group in the arts
Evidence of her distinction — press, client work, reviews, Fiverr reputation, commissioned projects
The kids: Spouses and unmarried children under 21 can apply for O-3 visas to accompany the main O-1B holder. They come with her. O-3 allows them to study in the US but not work.

Two questions here — the L-1 visa angle, and finding an attorney. Let me be direct on both.
On the L-1 — unfortunately this likely doesn't work for your situation.
The L-1 requires the company to sponsor a foreign national who has worked for a related company outside the US for at least one year in the last three years, and a clear parent, subsidiary, or affiliate relationship between the foreign and US companies must be established.
DNA LLC is a single Wyoming entity. There's no separate foreign company with a qualifying relationship to it. The L-1 is designed for multinationals moving employees between offices — it requires two distinct legal entities with at least 50% common ownership. You'd essentially need to formally establish a foreign branch or affiliate of the LLC, which is a real corporate structure exercise, not just paperwork. Worth asking an attorney whether that's feasible, but it's not a quick path.

You can search by location, language, and practice area. Filter for O-1, employment-based immigration, and Russian-speaking.

1. LLC Address Change
Two separate things need updating — Wyoming Secretary of State, and the IRS.
For Wyoming: you cannot change your LLC's principal business address or its mailing address via the Articles of Amendment — those require separate forms. ZenBusiness can handle this. ZenBusiness offers amendment filing services. Filing an amendment costs $100 plus any required state filing fees, unless you use an available amendment credit from Worry-Free Compliance. Log into ZenBusiness and look for the address change option — it's likely under the compliance or amendments section.
For the IRS: Form 8822-B is already filled and ready in business/forms/. That just needs to be mailed to IRS Kansas City MO 64999. This one can't be done through ZenBusiness.

2. Operating Agreement Amendment — Guaranteed Payment Structure
The $80,000/year ($6,666.67/month) priority payment to Ana is a guaranteed payment — it's already what you've been doing operationally and what was reported on the tax return. Formalizing it in the operating agreement is the right move.
Good news: in Wyoming, the operating agreement cannot be filed with the state — members simply sign the updated or revised agreement to make it an official binding contract. No state filing required. ZenBusiness can help draft the amendment for a fee, or it can be drafted directly. This is an internal document only.

4. Your Role and SSA Compliance — This Is the Most Important Item
Your $1,200 figure is actually the trial work period threshold, not the SGA limit. The SGA limit in 2026 is $1,690 per month gross for non-blind SSDI recipients. The trial work period threshold — the lower number — is $1,210/month in 2026.
But here's the critical point for self-employed LLC members: for the self-employed, SSA does not just look at income. SSA will find that your services are significant if you either contribute more than half of the total time needed to manage the business each month, or you manage the company for more than 45 hours in a month.
This means your income from the LLC is secondary. What matters to SSA is how many hours you're putting in and what function you're serving. If you're spending 50+ hours a month on client communications, strategy, and business management — that's the problem, regardless of what you're paid.

What context affects this agreement:
Wyoming LLC — Wyoming has very favorable LLC laws, strong charging order protection, and minimal disclosure requirements. The agreement should lean into Wyoming's flexibility rather than defaulting to generic boilerplate
NC principal address — doesn't affect Wyoming governance, but should be consistent throughout

On the $6,500/month justification:
It doesn't strictly need justification in the document — operating agreements typically just state the amount. But a brief recital is good practice and protects the arrangement if questioned. Your instinct about Ana's labor is right but "cartography business" undersells it. Here's a better framing:
The Members acknowledge that Anastasiia Yurievna Krasavina provides substantially all of the Company's creative services, including illustration, cartography, and digital art production, which constitute the primary source of the Company's revenue. The Guaranteed Payment is intended to compensate her for these services rendered to the Company prior to any allocation of profits.
This is clean, factual, and mirrors how the IRS expects guaranteed payments to be justified — as compensation for services, not as a profit share.
On Doug's role — "investor" framing:
The word "investor" in an LLC context is technically imprecise — you're a member, not an investor. But the concept you want is "non-participating member" or better: "capital member" versus Ana as the "services member." Some agreements use the term "passive member" explicitly. Given your SSA situation, the right framing is:
Douglas Michael Rubino serves as a capital-contributing member whose participation in the Company is limited to strategic oversight, capital management, and business administration. He does not perform services constituting the Company's primary business activities.
This is honest, accurate, and creates the right record for SSA purposes without being so passive that it suggests you have no role at all.

To your questions directly:
The guaranteed payment structure comes from IRC §707(c), which defines guaranteed payments as those made to a partner in exchange for services, determined without regard to the income of the partnership. The key legal requirement is that the amount is fixed — not contingent on whether the LLC makes money. $6,500/month qualifies because it's owed regardless of revenue.
Does it need justification? Not legally. But a brief recital protects the arrangement if it's ever questioned, and it establishes the business rationale. The best framing isn't "cartography business" — that undersells it and sounds like a separate company. The cleaner version:
The Guaranteed Payment is established in recognition that the Company's revenue-generating activities consist substantially of creative services — including illustration, cartography, and digital art — performed by Anastasiia Yurievna Krasavina. This payment compensates her for those services prior to any distribution of profits to either Member.
On framing Doug's role — the established distinction in LLC law is between members who perform services in their capacity as members versus members who contribute capital. The preferred terms are "Services-Contributing Member" and "Capital-Contributing Member." This is more precise than "investor" and creates the right legal record for SSA purposes without implying Doug has no role at all.

2*M, id='main') doc.addPageTemplates([PageTemplate(id='main', frames=frame)]) # Add signature block as flowable content sig_style = ParagraphStyle('sig_label', fontName='Times-Bold', fontSize=11, leading=14, spaceAfter=8, spaceBefore=0) name_style = ParagraphStyle('sig_name', fontName='Times-Roman', fontSize=10.5, leading=14, spaceAfter=5, textColor=colors.HexColor('#333333')) date_style = ParagraphStyle('sig_date', fontName='Times-Roman', fontSize=10.5, leading=14) from reportlab.platypus import Flowable class SignatureBlock(Flowable): def __init__(self, label, name, date, img_buf, img_orig_w, img_orig_h, render_w, move_down_frac=0.0, scale=1.0): super().__init__() self.label = label self.name = name self.date = date self.img_buf = img_buf self.img_orig_w = img_orig_w self.img_orig_h = img_orig_h self.render_w = render_w * scale self.render_h = (img_orig_h / img_orig_w) * render_w * scale self.move_down_frac = move_down_frac self._height = 14 + 64 + 6 + 14 + 14 + 16 # label + sig area + name + date + gap def draw(self): c = self.canv y = self._height - 14 # start from top # Label c.setFont('Times-Bold', 11) c.drawString(0, y, self.label) y -= 56 # sig area height # Sig line c.setLineWidth(0.5) c.line(0, y, CW, y) # Place signature image drop = self.render_h * self.move_down_frac img_y = y + 2 - drop # sit just above/on line self.img_buf.seek(0) c.drawImage(self.img_buf, 0, img_y, width=self.render_w, height=self.render_h, mask='auto', preserveAspectRatio=True) y -= 8 # Name c.setFont('Times-Roman', 10.5) c.setFillColor(colors.HexColor('#333333')) c.drawString(0, y, self.name) y -= 16 # Date c.setFillColor(colors.black) c.drawString(0, y, f'Date: {self.date}') c.setLineWidth(0.5) c.line(42, y - 2, 220, y - 2) def wrap(self, aw, ah): return CW, self._height # Doug: 691x180 original. Render at 210pt wide. Move down 20% of height. doug_render_w = 210 doug_render_h = (180/691) * 210 # ~54.7pt # Scale=1, move_down = 0.20 # Ana: 427x330 original. Render at 2x a base of 90pt wide = 180pt. Scale=2. ana_render_w = 90 # scale=2 applied in constructor story_with_sigs = story + [ sp(12), SignatureBlock('MEMBER:', 'Douglas Michael Rubino', 'May 9, 2026', doug_buf, 691, 180, doug_render_w, move_down_frac=0.20), sp(20), SignatureBlock('MEMBER:', 'Anastasiia Yurievna Krasavina', 'May 9, 2026', ana_buf, 427, 330, ana_render_w, move_down_frac=0.0, scale=2.0), ] doc.build(story_with_sigs) print("PDF generated") build_pdf() EOF

That's a clean reportlab-generated PDF with the signatures placed directly rather than going through HTML rendering. Doug's signature is dropped 20% of its height so it sits on the line. Ana's is 2x the base size.
On your question about whether this is a minimal, sane, useful operating agreement: Yes. Here's why I think so:
It specifies the Guaranteed Payment precisely because that's the entire reason the document exists. It specifies 50/50 interests because that's a fact. It has transfer restrictions because without them Wyoming defaults may not protect you the way you want. It has a deadlock provision because 50/50 with no resolution mechanism and Wyoming's default outcome being dissolution is genuinely dangerous. Everything else defers to the Act. There's nothing in it that over-commits either of you to a role, an amount of capital, or a mode of contribution that you didn't already agree to.
A human lawyer doing this for two people who trust each other and need something real but not over-engineered would write something close to this.

They're JFIF (JPEG format), not PNG - the upload converted them. There's no alpha channel, just black backgrounds. The signature strokes are very slightly brighter than the background (Doug's max brightness is 84/255, Ana's is 181/255). All my processing was wrong because I was inverting images that didn't need inverting and then losing the faint stroke detail.
The right approach: threshold - treat near-black pixels as background (make white), treat anything brighter as ink (make black). Clean binary result.

What changed: the upload converted your transparent PNGs to JPEG, replacing transparent pixels with black. Rather than inverting or adjusting brightness, I now do a simple threshold — any pixel with brightness above 10 out of 255 is ink (rendered black), anything at or below is the converted-transparency background (rendered transparent). Binary, no processing artifacts, no hollow middles. The ink stays as clean black strokes on the transparent layer which sits on your white document.
Ana's signature is 2x the base size and dropped 25% of its height to keep the center in the same position. Doug's is dropped 20% to sit on the line.
If the signatures still look off, the cleanest long-term fix is to re-export them from Photoshop as actual PNG files rather than JPEG — the upload is stripping the transparency on the way in.

I understand now exactly. The upload converted your PNG to JPEG — transparent pixels became black (0,0,0), ink pixels stayed dark. Both are near-black, just slightly different. The problem with my approach is I'm using proportional alpha, so ink pixels with brightness 20-80 out of 255 get low alpha values and appear faint.
Fix: threshold at 4 (cleanly separates background at 0-2 from ink at 5+), and make all ink pixels fully opaque. The ink WAS near-black in your original, so I'll keep it near-black with full opacity.
Ran python3 << 'PYEOF' from PIL import Image import numpy as np, io def make_sig_crisp(path, threshold=4): img = Image.open(path).convert('L') arr = np.array(img) rgba = np.zeros((arr.shape[0], arr.shape[1], 4), dtype=np.uint8) ink = arr > threshold # Ink: fully opaque, dark color preserving original values ink_brightness = arr[ink] # Normalize so faintest ink maps to dark gray, not transparent max_b = ink_brightness.max() if ink_brightness.size > 0 else 1 # Inverted: original ink (slightly bright against black bg) → dark ink on white ink_gray = (255 - (ink_brightness.astype(np.float32) / max_b * 180)).astype(np.uint8) rgba[ink, 0] = ink_gray rgba[ink, 1] = ink_gray rgba[ink, 2] = ink_gray rgba[ink, 3] = 255 # fully opaque rgba[~ink] = [255, 255, 255, 0] # transparent background result = Image.fromarray(rgba, 'RGBA') buf = io.BytesIO() result.save(buf, format='PNG') buf.seek(0) return buf # Preview: save test images to check for name, path in [('doug', '/mnt/user-data/uploads/Doug.png'), ('ana', '/mnt/user-data/uploads/Ana_Signature.png')]: buf = make_sig_crisp(path) with open(f'/home/claude/sig_test_{name}.png', 'wb') as f: f.write(buf.getvalue()) print("Test images saved") PYEOF

Ran python3 << 'PYEOF' from PIL import Image import numpy as np, io def make_sig(path, threshold=4): img = Image.open(path).convert('L') arr = np.array(img) ink = arr > threshold rgba = np.zeros((arr.shape[0], arr.shape[1], 4), dtype=np.uint8) rgba[~ink] = [255, 255, 255, 0] # transparent background if ink.sum() > 0: b = arr[ink].astype(float) # Normalize full range: min_ink → white (faint edge), max_ink → black (strong stroke) lo, hi = b.min(), b.max() if hi > lo: normalized = (b - lo) / (hi - lo) # 0=faint edge, 1=strong stroke else: normalized = np.ones_like(b) gray = (255 - normalized * 220).astype(np.uint8) # 35 → 255 (dark to light) rgba[ink, 0] = gray rgba[ink, 1] = gray rgba[ink, 2] = gray rgba[ink, 3] = np.minimum(255, (normalized * 280)).astype(np.uint8) # alpha also proportional result = Image.fromarray(rgba, 'RGBA') buf = io.BytesIO() result.save(buf, format='PNG') buf.seek(0) return buf for name, path in [('doug', '/mnt/user-data/uploads/Doug.png'), ('ana', '/mnt/user-data/uploads/Ana_Signature.png')]: buf = make_sig(path) with open(f'/home/claude/sig_test_{name}.png', 'wb') as f: f.write(buf.getvalue()) print("Done") PYEOF # Preview both python3 -c " from PIL import Image img = Image.open('/home/claude/sig_test_doug.png') print('Doug:', img.size, img.mode) img = Image.open('/home/claude/sig_test_ana.png') print('Ana:', img.size, img.mode) "

Let me verify the current numbers before confirming anything — this matters too much to rely on memory.
Searched the web for “SSDI 2026 self-employed SGA trial work period thresholds LLC owner passive member rules”
Your understanding is correct. Here's the confirmed picture for 2026:
The three thresholds you need to know:
SGA limit: $1,690/month for non-blind. Trial Work Period threshold: $1,210/month.
Your understanding of the 9-month protection is correct. The Trial Work Period allows you to test your ability to work for at least 9 months. During your TWP, you receive full SSDI benefits no matter how much you earn, as long as you report your work activity. The TWP continues until you accumulate nine service months within a rolling 60-month period. The months do not have to be consecutive.
A month counts as a TWP service month if your earnings exceed $1,210, or for self-employed individuals, if you work more than 80 hours in a month.
On the business itself: Passive income does not count toward SGA. The SSA only considers income earned from active work, such as wages from a job or net earnings from self-employment.
The critical self-employment wrinkle: SSA doesn't just look at income for self-employed people. They also evaluate hours worked and the value of services provided. The 80-hours-per-month trigger is the key number for you — if you stay under that, a month doesn't count as a TWP service month regardless of income.
For your specific situation: You made $0 from the LLC in 2025. The LLC distributes all revenue to Ana via guaranteed payment before you take anything. As long as your personal take from the LLC stays below $1,690/month, you're clear on SGA. And as long as you stay under 80 hours/month of involvement, you don't burn TWP months either.
The business is not a problem as structured — but report accurately to SSA when benefits start, and loop in your disability attorney before your first month of any income from the LLC.

Claude
20:03 UTC, 9 May 2026
Good question. The two numbers serve different purposes.
Under $1,210: Nothing happens. The month doesn't count toward anything. You're just earning below any threshold.
Between $1,210 and $1,690: The month counts as a Trial Work Period service month — it burns one of your nine. But you keep your full benefit check. No penalty, just a month used.
Above $1,690: Same as between $1,210 and $1,690 during the TWP — you still get paid, still burn a month. The difference only matters after your nine months are used up. Once the TWP is exhausted, earning above $1,690 in a month means benefits stop for that month.
So the $1,210 threshold isn't "you lose benefits" — it's just "this month counts toward your nine." The $1,690 is the actual cliff, but it only kicks in once you've burned through all nine TWP months.
Think of it as: $1,210 is the counter. $1,690 is the switch. The switch doesn't flip until the counter hits nine.
For your situation the practical target is staying under $1,210, because that way you never burn any of your nine months, and you preserve the full TWP as a safety net indefinitely.

After all nine TWP months are used:
Under $1,690: benefits continue
Over $1,690: benefits stop for that month

That's actually a reasonable cause argument, not FTA. For FTA you don't need to explain anything — you just ask for it. Here's exactly what to say:
When the agent picks up:
"Hi, I'm calling about a CP162A penalty notice for a partnership return. I'd like to request first-time penalty abatement."
They'll ask you to verify identity. Have ready:
EIN: 33-4868229
Business name: Digital Narrative Art LLC
Your name as responsible party
The notice number from the CP162A
The tax year: 2025
After you verify:
"This is the first year the partnership existed. We have no prior penalty history. I'm requesting first-time abatement under the IRS administrative waiver."
That's it. Don't explain why it was late. Don't mention April 15th. Don't mention anything about thinking the deadline was different. FTA doesn't require a reason — the moment you start giving reasons you're shifting into reasonable cause territory, which is harder and slower.
The agent will either approve it on the spot or say it needs to be reviewed. If approved, ask them to confirm the penalty is being abated and get a confirmation number.
If they say FTA doesn't apply:
"Can you tell me why it doesn't qualify? The entity had no prior penalties, all returns are filed, and there's no tax owed."
If still denied, don't argue. Say thank you, hang up, and we escalate to a written reasonable cause request via Form 843. But that's unlikely — first-year entity FTA is nearly automatic.
